column1: What was Sivers's fundamental mistake when deciding to rewrite CD Baby in Rails?
column2: He thought Rails was intrinsically better than PHP, but the language difference mattered far less than the business cost of a full rewrite.
column3: He spent 2 years on a Rails rewrite that got less than halfway done, then rewrote it himself in PHP in 2 months.

column1: What cost did Sivers avoid by rewriting in PHP instead of Rails?
column2: The "One Big Day" cost — retraining 85 employees, converting all cron scripts and internal tools simultaneously, and fielding furious customer calls about a completely new system.
column3: He could launch in stages, slowly gutting ugly PHP and replacing it, with no big re-training.

column1: What was the first question Sivers asked when abandoning the Rails rewrite?
column2: Is there anything Rails can do, that PHP can't do? — and the answer was no.
column3: This question cut through the emotional attachment to the newer language.

column1: What accounted for Sivers's perception that Ruby/Rails was superior to PHP?
column2: He was comparing his old ugly PHP code (written years earlier) against his new beautiful Rails code — but he was a much better programmer now.
column3: It's not the language (entirely). It's you. You're better now.

column1: How did Sivers's Rails experience still improve his PHP rewrite?
column2: He brought back MVC separation, Active Record models, autoloading, RESTful controllers, and a templating system — all applied in PHP.
column3: The PHP rewrite was 12,000 lines vs the original 90,000 — "the most beautiful PHP I've ever written."

column1: Why did Sivers prefer a custom PHP system over Rails's full framework?
column2: He uses maybe 10% of Rails; a custom system contains only what is absolutely necessary, making him "extremely happy and comfortable."
column3: Every line in his custom system exists because he needed it.

column1: How did the Rails rewrite's performance compare to the PHP rewrite?
column2: The PHP rewrite ran on a single 2U server serving CD Baby's traffic with hardly any load — no framework overhead.
column3: Small and fast wins over big and featureful when you only need a fraction of the features.

column1: Why did Sivers fight against Rails's ActiveRecord migrations?
column2: He loves SQL, thinks in tables and queries, and migrations hid SQL from him — the abstraction was friction, not relief.
column3: I dream in queries. I think in tables.

column1: What is Sivers's "girlfriend" analogy for programming languages?
column2: The new language feels better not because it is objectively better, but because you are a better programmer now — and you're comparing your old bad code to your new good code.

column1: What was the practical business reason Sivers could not do a One Big Day Rails cutover?
column2: The entire company's intranet, storefront, member login, and dozens of cron scripts were in PHP — all would have to change simultaneously, impossible without massive disruption.
column3: 85 employees would need retraining; customers would be furious.

column1: How does Sivers contrast adapting to a framework vs building your own?
column2: With Rails he had to hack plugins and mods to fit his existing 95-table multi-lingual database; with PHP he told it exactly what he wanted, the way he wanted it.
column3: I don't need to adapt my ways to PHP. I tell PHP exactly what I want to do.

column1: Under what condition would Sivers use Rails again?
column2: When starting a brand new project from scratch, with Rails in mind from the beginning — not retrofitting an existing system.
column3: The mistake was not Rails itself; it was using Rails to rewrite an existing PHP system with incompatible assumptions.
